Laïcité au Québec: nouvelle foi national: Secularism in Quebec: a new national faith?
Peut-on encore être croyant au Québec en: Can you still be a believer in Quebec in 2025? Religious freedom & secularism
Groupe de croyantes en prière. Courtoisi: Group of women believers in prayer. Courtesy: Église Impact Centre Chrétien
En ce moment, un sujet brûle toutes les: Right now, one subject is on everyone’s lips in faith communities: François Legault’s CAQ government is preparing a bill to ban prayer in public spaces. After first raising the idea in December, the premier seems ready to act. In doing so, he has set off a heated debate about religious freedom in a secular Quebec.
Au départ, nous voulions nous concentrer: At first, we wanted to focus solely on street prayer. But very quickly, the subject widened: can you still be openly religious in 2025? Between the elimination of the Ethics and Religious Culture course and the adoption of Bill 21, many worshippers feel the state’s secularism project is becoming more and more restrictive, to the point of wondering whether Quebec is turning atheism into a religion.
Pour ce reportage, nous avons rencontré: For this story, we met members of different communities: an evangelical missionary whose family left Morocco to escape religious pressure and who now worries about seeing the same restrictions here; a pastor; a protester who prays in the street in support of Gaza; an imam; and experts on the issue. They all agree on one point: fundamental rights are at stake, and the debate is being heavily exploited for political purposes.
Par manque de temps, nous n’avons pas pu: Due to lack of time, we were unable to include other perspectives, notably that of the Jewish community, which we would have liked to hear from.
‍<strong>Le gouvernement caquiste de Fra: ‍François Legault’s CAQ government is preparing a bill to ban prayer in public spaces. After raising the idea last December, the premier seems ready to make this restriction official, prompting a wide-ranging debate about religious freedom in a secular Quebec. La Converse met with people who live this reality every day, including members of the Muslim and evangelical Christian communities. For them, one question arises: how do you practise your religion in 2025?
À 25 ans, Sara*, qui est d’origine maroc: At 25, Sara*, who is of Moroccan origin, lives a life very different from that of other young professionals her age. As a Christian missionary, she regularly travels the world to spread the Gospel. With long brown hair and a headset on, the young woman speaks to us by video call. When she isn’t travelling, she can be found on the streets of Montréal, alone or with members of the Revival Montreal movement, evangelizing, that is, sharing her faith and praying for strangers.
Sara est née au Maroc, et sa famille a i: Sara was born in Morocco, and her family immigrated to Canada when she was six to escape the religious restrictions imposed on them, she says. “My father is an atheist and my mother is a Christian. Neither of them is Muslim,” she says. “In Morocco, you can be a Christian, but you’re not allowed to evangelize and pray for people in public. And during Ramadan, you’re not allowed to eat [in public] either. If you do, you risk prison,” says the young woman.
Pour cette famille marocaine, l’exil ava: For this Moroccan family, exile had a purpose: finding a country where religious freedom was more than a theoretical concept. “My story is the story of many immigrants. Canada didn’t attract our family only for its economic prosperity, but also for the possibility of living our faith without social pressure or persecution. That’s what we came here looking for,” Sara explains.
Mais aujourd’hui, la jeune missionnaire: But today, the young missionary is worried. For her, the bill banning prayer in public spaces puts Quebec on a dangerous slope. “If this law passes, there won’t be much difference between Quebec, Iran and North Korea,” she believes. “Why? Because if you start praying in the street, a police officer can come. In North Korea, if you pray in the street, a police officer comes too. It’s the same thing. It’s hard to hear, but deep down, the logic is the same: controlling what the population believes,” she says flatly.
Some experts share this view. Last December, political scientist Marc Chevrier <l1>told the outlet Présence:</l1> “Banning any public display of prayer is what we see in totalitarian states, where prayer was not only not tolerated but sometimes outright prohibited, as in the former Soviet Union or in China.”
<strong>« Être croyant en 2025, c’est po: “Being a believer in 2025 is possible if you make yourself very small”
Devant le centre Badr, réservé le vendre: In front of the Badr centre, which is reserved for Muslim worshippers on Fridays, Nour, a 24-year-old Quebecer and Muslim, directs cars in and out of a parking lot that is too small for the crowd of worshippers. Prayer has just ended. The men and women leave through separate doors.
« Dans notre religion, on apprend à être: “In our religion, we learn to be discreet, not to disturb other people’s peace. So praying outside isn’t a common practice. In a country where the majority isn’t Muslim, we shouldn’t impose ourselves that way, even for a good reason,” he begins. According to the young man, this discretion is necessary to protect the image of his community, which he believes is distorted.
Il pointe notamment le rôle des médias e: He points in particular to the role of the media and of education. He remembers his school years, when the Ethics and Religious Culture course fostered open-mindedness and tolerance. “We visited Hindu temples, mosques, churches, synagogues… We learned about all the religions. It helped a lot of students understand and respect other beliefs,” he recalls. But since last year, the course has disappeared from the curriculum, replaced by Ethics and Quebec Culture.
Solange Lefebvre, professeure et titulai: Solange Lefebvre, a professor and holder of the Research Chair in Managing Cultural and Religious Diversity who took part in developing the Ethics and Religious Culture course, doesn’t mince words. “[The government] replaced the Ethics and Religious Culture program, which had cost tens of millions of dollars and required an enormous amount of design and reflection work over a period of 10 to 12 years, with a course on citizenship and then on Quebec identity. It’s pure manipulation!” she exclaims.
« Être croyant en 2025, c’est possible s: “Being a believer in 2025 is possible if you make yourself very small,” Nour continues. “Especially if you’re Muslim.” But he says a ban on prayer in public spaces would have little effect on how Muslims practise. “Apart from those who protest, nobody prays in public spaces,” he says flatly.
C’est le cas de Zahraa, 25 ans, étudiant: That is the case for Zahraa, 25, a student at Université de Montréal. For more than two years, she has protested every week against the genocide in Gaza. For her, praying in the street has become an act of collective resistance and of communion among several communities.
<em>« </em>Quand on prie ensemble après: “When we pray together after the protests, it’s not only Muslims in the prayers; there are Christians, there are Jews, there are atheists. We even translate the prayers so that everyone can take part. These are things anyone can share: we pray for orphaned children, for the people of Gaza to be freed, for their suffering to end soon.”
Elle insiste : les prières de rue ne son: She insists that street prayers are simply the result of circumstances. “In Islam, we have prescribed prayer times. When the time comes, no matter where we are, we pray. When we protest, we’re already occupying public space. The only difference is that instead of standing, we kneel, we prostrate ourselves,” she explains.
Elle observe que les critiques qui fusen: She observes that the criticism flying around doesn’t come from any real disturbance, but from Islamophobic prejudice fuelled by the dominant discourse. “The government and the mainstream media have shaped the image of believers a great deal, especially Muslims and the veil. The result: people are almost afraid of us.”
Elle déplore qu’il y ait deux poids, deu: She laments the double standard: “When it’s Christians praying in the street, it’s never presented as a problem in the media. But Muslim prayers are quickly singled out. Yet we’re not bothering anyone!” she says flatly.

<em>«Avant, c’était \"Habille-toi comme: “Before, it was ‘Dress like a white woman’; today, it’s ‘Behave like a white woman.’ Prostrating yourself in the street isn’t considered Québécois.” -Zeinab Diab
Le fait qu’il y ait deux poids, deux mes: The double standard, which Zahraa and other believers decry, is part of a broader context, explains Zeinab Diab, an expert in religious studies. A specialist in Bill 21, she devoted her thesis to studying the law’s effects on religious minorities in Quebec. For her, the new bill has a clear goal: “Feeding fear of the Muslim enemy.”
Elle rappelle à cet égard la définition: In this regard, she recalls the definition of Islamophobia, which is not limited to individual prejudice. “Islamophobia is a political system that aims to dominate Muslim communities,” she begins.
“People talk about Muslims all the time. It started with the bodies of Muslim women, with the veil, and now they’re going after behaviour. Before, it was ‘Dress like a white woman’; today, it’s ‘Behave like a white woman.’ Prostrating yourself in the street isn’t considered Québécois…” She pauses before continuing vehemently. “These people are praying for their brothers and sisters in Gaza and Lebanon, who have been massacred for two years and whose mutilated bodies parade across our screens every day. Praying as a group is a form of renewal that eases collective trauma, it’s peaceful,” she insists.
« On disait viser tous les signes religi: “They said they were targeting all religious symbols, but everyone knew it was the hijab. Today, they claim to target all religions, but everyone knows it’s Muslims who are being targeted,” she hammers home.
Un constat renforcé par <l1>le rapport P: This view is reinforced by <l1>the Pelchat-Rousseau report</l1>, published barely a few days before the premier proposed a bill to ban street prayer. In that document, Muslims are mentioned more than 30 times and Islam more than 20 times, twice as often as all the other religions combined.
Pour sa part, la sociologue Solange Lefe: For her part, sociologist Solange Lefebvre wants to point out that other faiths have also been hit hard by measures linked to state secularism, notably Catholicism, historically the majority religion in Quebec. “The Catholic Church has lost a lot of prerogatives,” she says. “Masses held at the end of January are no longer recognized. They were banned from the public sphere so that they’d be private, held in certain places. The Catholic Church has paid the price too.” In practice,<l1> all religions could indeed be affected by such a measure.</l1>
« C’est faisable, mais difficile. » Voil: “It’s doable, but difficult.” That is the answer from Hassan Guillet, an imam and founding member of the Table interreligieuse de concertation Québec, when asked whether it is still possible, in his view, to practise one’s religion freely in Quebec.
Nous parlant depuis sa voiture, il dével: Speaking to us from his car, he elaborates. “More and more, they’re trying to make secularism a new religion. They’re trying to impose atheism, not secularism. Secularism is the equality of all believers and non-believers before the law,” he says, stressing the two concepts.
Sara abonde dans le même sens. Aux yeux: Sara agrees. In the missionary’s eyes, the neutrality invoked by the Quebec government actually conceals an ideology. “They say, ‘We’re secular, we’re just removing religion from public space.’ But in fact, it’s imposing atheism.”
Un sondage mené par la firme Léger et pu: A poll conducted by the firm Léger and published on September 11 indicates that 43% of respondents want street prayer banned in Quebec, compared with only 21% elsewhere in the country. Sébastien Dallaire, executive vice-president of Léger, explains this gap by the fact that <l1>Quebecers are, in general, much less religiously observant than the rest of the Canadian population</l1>.
<strong>Prières de rue : véritable farde: Street prayer: a real burden or a false debate in Quebec?
Le 11 septembre dernier, le ministre res: On September 11, the minister responsible for secularism, Jean-François Roberge, described in the Journal de Montréal a Quebec where spontaneous prayers were multiplying and obstructing access to public spaces. Yet the minister’s statement is not backed by any tangible evidence.
Quelques cas de prière dans l’espace pub: A few cases of prayer in public space have indeed made the news. Prayers held this summer in front of Notre-Dame Basilica in Montréal, as part of pro-Palestinian protests, notably provoked strong reactions both among the public and in the political sphere. La Converse, however, was unable to find solid evidence or quantitative studies to conclude that street prayer causes systematic, measurable disruption.
Quelques jours avant que le premier mini: A few days before the premier raised the idea of a bill to ban street prayer, the Pelchat-Rousseau report was published and welcomed by Minister Roberge. The report does not recommend such a ban. Its co-chair, Christiane Pelchat, recipient of the 2022 Prix de la laïcité Guy-Rocher, says on the contrary that these prayers are not a problem in Montréal. Regarding the prayer in front of Notre-Dame Basilica, she offered the following nuance in the article cited above: <l1>“It seems to be mostly a political prayer, supporting the Palestinian cause, rather than real street prayer among believers.”</l1>

Sara, de son côté, est d’avis que le déb: Sara, for her part, believes the debate goes beyond Quebec: it touches the heart of fundamental rights. “Our human right is the freedom to choose what we believe. But if the government tells you, ‘You don’t have the right to pray here,’ it takes that choice away. It’s as if your freedom were confiscated,” she says, raising her eyebrows.
Maryse Potvin, une politologue qui a con: Maryse Potvin, a political scientist whose research has focused on the effects of Bill 21 on Quebec universities, agrees: “They’re going to attack forms of freedom of expression, and freedom of religion, which can be closely tied to freedom of expression [...] It’s not usually the Quebec state that manages these issues [protests in streets and parks], but municipalities. So this changes the game completely.”
« La CAQ veut que la foi soit de plus en: “The CAQ wants faith to be increasingly restricted to the private sphere, meaning the home and places of worship, when it has never been delimited that way,” she says.
Andrew Cho, lui, ne se sent pas concerné: Andrew Cho, for his part, doesn’t feel concerned. He has been evangelizing on the streets of Montréal for more than five years and has more than 15,000 followers on Instagram, where he posts evangelism videos daily. He draws a distinction between prayer and evangelism. “The Bible tells me to pray in private. Evangelizing and praying in public space are not the same thing,” he explains.
Quand on lui rappelle qu’il prie parfois: When reminded that he sometimes prays for passersby, he acknowledges that the question could be sensitive. “If they ban evangelism, talking about Jesus, then it could have an effect. And I would be against that law. But it’s nothing new: even in the time of the apostles, the authorities banned the proclamation of the Word of God. The question was clear: whom should we obey? Men or God?” he says, certain of his decision.
Il ajoute qu’aucune restriction législat: He adds that no legislative restriction will change his practice: “For me, nothing will change. I’m going to keep evangelizing and praying for those who want it.”
Pour Maryse Potvin, la loi 21 n’est pas: For Maryse Potvin, Bill 21 is not merely a measure to strengthen secularism but a strategy of political exploitation.
Elle rappelle qu’à son arrivée au pouvoi: She recalls that when the CAQ came to power, it made this law one of its priorities: “We were coming out of a context marked by the Quebec City mosque attack and the growing visibility of ultranationalist groups like La Meute, the Soldiers of Odin and the Fédération des Québécois de souche. These groups had radicalized around the debate on secularism and religious symbols. The CAQ chose to adopt Bill 21 to calm things down and send them a signal.”
Ce choix a été stratégique, explique-t-e: That choice was strategic, she explains: “It was a way of responding to populist identity groups, which had been demanding greater state secularism since the Bouchard-Taylor commission and the Quebec Charter of Values. After Bill 21, we saw some of these groups disappear or lose visibility.”
Mais au-delà de cette apparente pacifica: But beyond this apparent pacification, she now sees an electoral exploitation of the issue: “Talking about street prayer now is a way of diverting attention from the government’s real failures: the health care crisis, education, the SAAQ fiasco, or the billions sunk into failed projects like the third link. Instead of fixing these problems, they create a diversion because elections are coming. And since the PQ seems to be rising in voting intentions, now they’re playing the nationalist card.”
Cette analyse est partagée par Hassan Gu: Hassan Guillet shares this analysis. “We have so many problems to fix, notably in our health care system, which isn’t in good health,” he laments, accusing politicians of diverting attention for “purely electoral” purposes and of targeting certain communities to woo other voters.
Zeinab Diab dresse le même constat : « C: Zeinab Diab reaches the same conclusion: “What is presented as a problem isn’t one,” she insists. “There has never been a complaint, not a single incident linked to prayer. But they blow it up in public debate, they manufacture a sense of urgency, they keep repeating that there’s a danger. This fixation on Muslim communities means the government isn’t dealing with real problems and is diverting attention from the real issues: health, education, housing.”
L’appel de Sara est clair : que le Québe: Sara’s call is clear: that Quebec show humility. “As a Christian, I learned that we must honour and value all cultures. That doesn’t mean agreeing on everything, but recognizing the worth of others. The danger is pride, telling yourself, ‘Our culture is better, our vision is the right one.’ The majority of Quebecers are atheists, fine. But that doesn’t give them the right to impose that vision on minorities. Otherwise, we’re repeating the same flaws as the countries that try to control their people’s religion.”
« Et vous, que feriez-vous ? Si vous avi: “And you, what would you do? If you had left your native country to escape a lack of religious freedom, or any other form of constraint, and once you arrived in your new country, you were told that the same government pressure was catching up with you again?” she asks, addressing our readers directly.
Zahraa, de son côté, redoute une dérive: Zahraa, for her part, fears an authoritarian drift: “It’s not the fact that street prayer is under threat that scares me. But if we accept today that this freedom is taken from us, what will be banned tomorrow?”
En guise de mot de la fin, Hassan Guille: For a final word, Hassan Guillet wants to leave one last thought: “All these protests were meant to draw attention to the genocide happening before our eyes in Gaza and to the deaths of thousands of children. It’s a real international problem. I find that, unfortunately, the debates have been hijacked and all centred on prayer in the street, instead of talking about the genocide in Gaza, the violation of human rights and of international law,” he concludes.
